original_value: More consistent and current estimates of forest land cover type and forest structural metrics are needed to guide national policies on forest management, carbon sequestration, and ecosystem health. In recent years, the increased availability of high-resolution (<30 m) imagery and advancements in machine learning algorithms have opened up a new opportunity to fuse multiple datasets of varying spatial, spectral, and temporal resolutions. Here, we present a new model, based on a deep learning architecture, that performs both classification and regression concurrently, thereby consolidating what was previously several independent tasks and models into one stream. The model, a multi-task recurrent convolutional neural network that we call the Chimera, integrates varying resolution, freely available aerial and satellite imagery, as well as relevant environmental factors (e.g., climate, terrain) to simultaneously classify five forest cover types (‘conifer’, ‘deciduous’, ‘mixed’, ‘dead’, ‘none’ (non-forest)) and to estimate four continuous forest structure metrics (above ground biomass, quadratic mean diameter, basal area, canopy cover). We demonstrate the performance of our approach by training an ensemble of Chimera models on 9967 georeferenced (true locations) Forest Inventory and Analysis field plots from the USDA Forest Service within California and Nevada. Classification diagnostics for the Chimera ensemble on an independent test set produces an overall average precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.92, 0.92, and 0.92. Class-wise F1-scores were high for ‘none’ (0.99) and ‘conifer’ (0.85) cover classes, and moderate for the ‘mixed’ (0.74) class samples. This demonstrates a strong ability to discriminate locations with and without trees. Regression diagnostics on the test set indicate very high accuracy for ensembled estimates of above ground biomass (     R 2  = 0.84 ,     RMSE     = 37.28     Mg/ha), quadratic mean diameter (     R 2  = 0.81 ,     RMSE     = 3.74     inches), basal area (     R 2  = 0.87 ,     RMSE     = 25.88     ft     2    /ac), and canopy cover (     R 2  = 0.89 ,     RMSE     = 8.01     percent). Comparative analysis of the Chimera ensemble versus support vector machine and random forest approaches demonstrates increased performance over both methods. Future implementations of the Chimera ensemble on a distributed computing platform could provide continuous, annual estimates of forest structure for other forested landscapes at regional or national scales.

result.paraphrase: We need more up-to-date and consistent estimates of forest land-cover type and forest structural metrics to inform national forest management, carbon sequestration, and ecosystem health policies. Recent growth in high-resolution (<30 m) imagery availability, together with advances in machine learning, has created a new opportunity to merge multiple datasets with different spatial, spectral, and temporal resolutions. In this study, we introduce a new deep learning-based model that carries out classification and regression at the same time, combining what were previously several separate tasks and models into one pipeline. The model, a multi-task recurrent convolutional neural network we call Chimera, integrates imagery of varying resolution from freely available aerial and satellite sources along with relevant environmental variables such as climate and terrain to simultaneously classify five forest cover types—conifer, deciduous, mixed, dead, and none (non-forest)—and estimate four continuous forest structure metrics: aboveground biomass, quadratic mean diameter, basal area, and canopy cover. We evaluate the method by training an ensemble of Chimera models on 9,967 georeferenced Forest Inventory and Analysis field plots from the USDA Forest Service in California and Nevada. On an independent test set, the Chimera ensemble achieves overall average precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.92, 0.92, and 0.92. Class-specific F1-scores are high for none (0.99) and conifer (0.85) cover classes, and moderate for mixed (0.74), showing strong discrimination between treed and treeless locations. Regression results on the test set show very high accuracy for ensembled estimates of aboveground biomass (R2 = 0.84, RMSE = 37.28 Mg/ha), quadratic mean diameter (R2 = 0.81, RMSE = 3.74 inches), basal area (R2 = 0.87, RMSE = 25.88 ft2/ac), and canopy cover (R2 = 0.89, RMSE = 8.01 percent). A comparison with support vector machine and random forest methods shows that the Chimera ensemble performs better than both. With implementation on a distributed computing platform, the Chimera ensemble could eventually provide continuous annual estimates of forest structure for other forested landscapes at regional or national scales.
